In my previous article, I wrote about the 'points that make you want to retort' that I felt while watching 'Marching Song: Marching Boys.' However, beyond those moments of discomfort, there were indeed moments in this film that moved me.

One of them is the 'breathtaking 7-minute performance at the end,' which was also touted in the trailer. I felt this scene was genuinely realistic. For someone like me who has watched my sons' competitions many times, the tension of that moment and the sensation of sound, light, and movement surging forward as one were undeniably authentic.

What left the strongest impression on me was the scene where the protagonist, who has no gymnastics experience, successfully lands a backflip during the actual performance. Of course, it might be an unlikely development in reality. However, as the emotional peak of the story, that scene certainly functioned well. The persuasiveness of 'this moment exists precisely because they have come this far'

And throughout this film, I think what moved me the most was not the performance itself, but the changes and growth in human relationships. The relationship between the father and Jiang Hao, the relationship between the teacher and the students, and the relationships among the club members—each slowly changes its shape within the story.

What was particularly impressive was the relationship between the teacher and the students. What each believed to be 'the best way' naturally moved toward a compromise as they learned of each other's feelings. Rather than forcibly resolving conflicts, the relationships changed as their understanding deepened—I was quietly moved by that careful depiction. I think the same can be said for the parent

Regarding the protagonist Jiang Hao, I also felt he was 'very much like a high school student.' Having walked the path his father told him to follow until now, and with his father even having a say in his future, he wavers between his own will and the path laid out for him. The actions and emotions born from that discrepancy were truly unique to this generation.
